segments.speaker: teacher
segments.text: Your plane has 100 eddy seats. The airline sells 185 tickets. No, nobody failed kindergarten. They did it on purpose because, on almost every route, some passengers cancel late or simply don't show up. And an empty seat has a brutal business model. The second the plane leaves, it becomes worth exactly zero.

segments.speaker: teacher
segments.text: Airlines know this, so their revenue systems study historical patterns and forecast how many booked passengers probably won't board. Imagine a 180-seat flight where the airline expects about five no-shows. Selling 185 tickets can still produce 180 actual humans. Perfect. Every seat occupied. Everybody happy. The spreadsheet gets a tiny promotion.

segments.speaker: teacher
segments.text: But predictions are not promises. If seven people vanish, two seats still fly empty. If exactly five disappear, the math looks genius. And if nobody disappears, congratulations. We now have 185 passengers and 180 seats. This is the moment a calm gate announcement suddenly starts sounding like an auction.

segments.speaker: teacher
segments.text: First, airlines may ask for volunteers to take a later flight in exchange for compensation. In the United States, the Department of Transportation requires airlines to seek volunteers before involuntarily denying boarding because of an oversale. Exact rules vary by country. This is why you sometimes hear the offer climb, $200, $400, and suddenly, somebody remembers they never liked this destination anyway.

segments.speaker: teacher
segments.text: So, why risk paying people at all? Because airlines are balancing two costs. Cost one, a seat leaves empty and can never be sold again. Cost two, too many people show up and the airline pays to fix the problem. The goal is not, sell as many tickets as possible. It's, sell just enough extra tickets that the expected empty seat loss is smaller than the expected overbooking cost.

segments.speaker: teacher
segments.text: And the number is not the same for every flight. A Monday morning business route may behave differently from a holiday flight. Airlines use demand forecasts, booking behavior, cancellations, and historical no-show patterns to decide how much overbooking, if any, a flight can tolerate. Some airlines don't oversell at all. The system is a forecast, not a rule.

segments.speaker: teacher
segments.text: So, the weird truth is this, airlines are not really selling chairs, they are managing probabilities around chairs. Your 22 Ayas is sitting inside a model that asks one question. How many of these booked humans will actually appear at the gate? Airlines don't overbook because they forgot to count, they overbook because they counted everyone, including the people they expect not to show up.
